description: 100 questions on OOP attributes (coding and logic based, intermediate/advanced level)

questions.question: class A: x = 1. Where does x live?
questions.answer:
class A: x = 1. x lives in the class's namespace, stored in A.__dict__ as a class attribute. All instances share this one value.

code:
class A:
    x = 1

print('x' in A.__dict__)

real example:
Shared settings like a tax rate live on the class, not on each object.

questions.question: class A: def __init__(self): self.y = 2. Where does y live?
questions.answer:
class A: def __init__(self): self.y = 2. y lives in each instance's own __dict__ as an instance attribute. Each object gets its own copy.

code:
class A:
    def __init__(self):
        self.y = 2

print(A().__dict__)

real example:
Each user account stores its own password hash in its instance dictionary.

questions.question: What is the main difference between a class attribute and an instance attribute?
questions.answer:
A class attribute is shared by all instances, while an instance attribute belongs to just one object. Assigning on the instance shadows the class value.

code:
class A:
    x = 1

a = A()
a.y = 2

real example:
A shared app theme versus per-user preferences.

questions.question: class A: x = 1. a = A(); b = A(). print(a.x == b.x) outputs?
questions.answer:
class A: x = 1. a = A(); b = A(). print(a.x == b.x) outputs True. Both instances read the same shared class attribute, so the values match.

code:
class A:
    x = 1

a = A()
b = A()
print(a.x == b.x)

real example:
All employees read the same company holiday list.

questions.question: class A: x = 1. a = A(); b = A(). print(a.x is b.x) outputs?
questions.answer:
class A: x = 1. a = A(); b = A(). print(a.x is b.x) outputs True. Both resolve to the very same class attribute object in memory.

code:
class A:
    x = 1

a = A()
b = A()
print(a.x is b.x)

real example:
Shared immutable constants are truly one object across all instances.

questions.question: class A: def __init__(self): self.x = 1. a=A(); b=A(). print(a.x is b.x) outputs?
questions.answer:
class A: def __init__(self): self.x = 1. print(a.x is b.x) outputs True for small ints because Python interns them, but each instance conceptually owns its own x.

code:
class A:
    def __init__(self):
        self.x = 1

a = A()
b = A()
print(a.x is b.x)

real example:
Treat values with ==, not is, except when you mean shared singletons.

questions.question: class A: x = 1. a = A(); a.x = 2. What does a.x return now?
questions.answer:
class A: x = 1. a = A(); a.x = 2. a.x returns 2. The new instance attribute shadows the class attribute for that object only.

code:
class A:
    x = 1

a = A()
a.x = 2
print(a.x)

real example:
A user's custom nickname overrides the default username just for them.

questions.question: In the setup above, what does A.x return?
questions.answer:
class A: x = 1. a = A(); a.x = 2. A.x returns 1. Assigning on the instance never touches the class attribute itself.

code:
class A:
    x = 1

a = A()
a.x = 2
print(A.x)

real example:
One person's theme override does not change the app-wide default.

questions.question: class A: x = 1. a=A(); a.x = 2; del a.x. What does a.x return?
questions.answer:
class A: x = 1. a=A(); a.x = 2; del a.x. a.x returns 1. Deleting the instance attribute re-exposes the class attribute underneath.

code:
class A:
    x = 1

a = A()
a.x = 2
del a.x
print(a.x)

real example:
Clearing a temporary override restores the platform default.

questions.question: class A: x = 1. a=A(); a.x = 2; del a.x. What does A.x return?
questions.answer:
class A: x = 1. a=A(); a.x = 2; del a.x. A.x returns 1. The class attribute was never modified by instance operations.

code:
class A:
    x = 1

a = A()
a.x = 2
del a.x
print(A.x)

real example:
Deleting a user preference does not affect the stored global default.

questions.question: class A: x = 1. a=A(); del a.x. What happens?
questions.answer:
class A: x = 1. a=A(); del a.x raises AttributeError. Since x is only a class attribute, there is nothing on the instance to delete.

code:
class A:
    x = 1

a = A()
del a.x

real example:
Trying to remove a non-existent override errors rather than silently passing.

questions.question: class A: data = []. a=A(); b=A(). a.data.append(5); print(b.data) outputs?
questions.answer:
class A: data = []. a=A(); b=A(). a.data.append(5); print(b.data) outputs [5]. A mutable class attribute is genuinely shared by all instances.

code:
class A:
    data = []

a = A()
a.data.append(5)
print(A().data)

real example:
A shared to-do list visible across all team members updates for everyone.

questions.question: class A: data = []. a=A(); a.data = [9]; b=A(). print(b.data) outputs?
questions.answer:
class A: data = []. a=A(); a.data = [9]; b=A(). print(b.data) outputs []. Rebinding only touches a's instance; others still see the class list.

code:
class A:
    data = []

a = A()
a.data = [9]
print(A().data)

real example:
Giving one team its own list does not change the shared company list.

questions.question: class A: data = []. a=A(); a.data.append(1); print(a.data is A.data) outputs?
questions.answer:
class A: data = []. a=A(); a.data.append(1); print(a.data is A.data) outputs True. Appending mutates the same list without creating a new one.

code:
class A:
    data = []

a = A()
a.data.append(1)
print(a.data is A.data)

real example:
Editing a shared spreadsheet cell updates the same file all views point to.

questions.question: class A: data = []. a=A(); a.data = a.data + [1]; print(a.data is A.data) outputs?
questions.answer:
class A: data = []. a=A(); a.data = a.data + [1]; print(a.data is A.data) outputs False. The + operator builds a new list and rebinds a.data.

code:
class A:
    data = []

a = A()
a.data = a.data + [1]
print(a.data is A.data)

real example:
Creating a revised copy of a document leaves the original untouched.

questions.question: How do you read an attribute whose name is in a string variable?
questions.answer:
Use getattr(obj, name) to read an attribute whose name is held in a string variable. It performs the normal attribute lookup by name.

code:
class A:
    def __init__(self):
        self.x = 1

name = 'x'
print(getattr(A(), name))

real example:
Forms map column names sent as strings onto object fields.

questions.question: How do you set an attribute whose name is computed at runtime?
questions.answer:
Use setattr(obj, name, value) to set an attribute computed at runtime. The name arrives as a string and the value is stored dynamically.

code:
class A:
    pass

a = A()
setattr(a, 'color', 'red')
print(a.color)

real example:
Importers write unknown fields directly from the data header names.

questions.question: How do you check if an object has an attribute?
questions.answer:
Use hasattr(obj, 'attr') to check whether an object has an attribute. It returns True when the name resolves anywhere in the lookup chain.

code:
class A:
    x = 1

print(hasattr(A(), 'x'))

real example:
Checking for optional metadata before printing it to a report.

questions.question: What does getattr(obj, 'missing', 42) return when missing isn't present?
questions.answer:
getattr(obj, 'missing', 42) returns 42 when the attribute is absent. The supplied default is returned instead of raising AttributeError.

code:
class A:
    pass

print(getattr(A(), 'missing', 42))

real example:
Missing settings fall back to a sensible default instead of crashing.

questions.question: What does hasattr(obj, 'missing') return when missing isn't present?
questions.answer:
hasattr(obj, 'missing') returns False when the attribute is absent. The name cannot be found anywhere in the lookup chain.

code:
class A:
    pass

print(hasattr(A(), 'missing'))

real example:
Deciding which UI sections to show based on which data exists.

questions.question: class A: pass. a=A(). What does getattr(a, 'x', 'n/a') return?
questions.answer:
class A: pass. a=A(). getattr(a, 'x', 'n/a') returns 'n/a'. There is no x anywhere, so the default value is handed back.

code:
class A:
    pass

print(getattr(A(), 'x', 'n/a'))

real example:
A profile page shows n/a when the preferred name has never been set.

questions.question: class A: x = 10. a = A(). What does getattr(a, 'x') return?
questions.answer:
class A: x = 10. a = A(). getattr(a, 'x') returns 10. getattr also sees class attributes during its lookup.

code:
class A:
    x = 10

print(getattr(A(), 'x'))

real example:
Reading shared config from an instance works transparently.

questions.question: How do you delete an attribute at runtime?
questions.answer:
Use delattr(obj, 'attr') or del obj.attr to delete an attribute at runtime. Both remove the named attribute from the object.

code:
class A:
    pass

a = A()
a.x = 1
delattr(a, 'x')
print(hasattr(a, 'x'))

real example:
Clearing cached results from an object before recomputing them.

questions.question: What does delattr(a, 'missing') raise?
questions.answer:
delattr(a, 'missing') raises AttributeError. There is no such attribute to delete, so Python reports it.

code:
class A:
    pass

a = A()
delattr(a, 'missing')

real example:
Clean-up code checks hasattr before attempting a deletion.

questions.question: What does a.__dict__ show for an object with only instance attributes?
questions.answer:
a.__dict__ shows a dictionary mapping attribute names to their values for a given instance. Only instance-level data appears there.

code:
class A:
    def __init__(self):
        self.x = 1

print(A().__dict__)

real example:
Serializers read __dict__ to dump objects to JSON.

questions.question: class A: def __init__(self): self.name = 'x'; self.age = 2. print(sorted(A().__dict__)) outputs?
questions.answer:
class A: def __init__(self): self.name = 'x'; self.age = 2. print(sorted(A().__dict__)) outputs ['age', 'name']. Sorting the dict keys alphabetically gives age then name.

code:
class A:
    def __init__(self):
        self.name = 'x'
        self.age = 2

print(sorted(A().__dict__))

real example:
Generating a stable, sorted list of a record's fields for reports.

questions.question: Can you set an attribute directly via the instance __dict__?
questions.answer:
Yes, you can set an attribute directly via the instance __dict__: a.__dict__['attr'] = value. This is equivalent to setattr.

code:
class A:
    pass

a = A()
a.__dict__['attr'] = 1
print(a.attr)

real example:
Low-level tools manipulate object storage directly for speed.

questions.question: class A: pass. a=A(); a.__dict__['z'] = 1; print(a.z) outputs?
questions.answer:
class A: pass. a=A(); a.__dict__['z'] = 1; print(a.z) outputs 1. The dictionary entry becomes an ordinary attribute.

code:
class A:
    pass

a = A()
a.__dict__['z'] = 1
print(a.z)

real example:
Decoding a flat map row into object attributes.

questions.question: What does vars(a) return?
questions.answer:
vars(a) returns the same dictionary as a.__dict__. Both expose the instance's attribute storage.

code:
class A:
    def __init__(self):
        self.x = 1

a = A()
print(vars(a) == a.__dict__)

real example:
Debugging helpers use vars to snapshot an object's current state.

questions.question: Does the instance __dict__ contain class attributes or methods?
questions.answer:
No, the instance __dict__ does not contain class attributes or methods. Those live on the class, keeping each instance dict focused on data.

code:
class A:
    x = 1

    def m(self):
        return 2

print(A().__dict__)

real example:
Confirming instance memory stays small and focused on that object's own data.

questions.question: What is the attribute lookup order for obj.name?
questions.answer:
For obj.name, Python checks obj.__dict__ first, then the class, then each parent class in the MRO, then raises AttributeError.

code:
class A:
    x = 1

a = A()
print(a.x)

real example:
This search order is why instance overrides shadow inherited defaults.

questions.question: class A: def method(self): return 1. What is A.Method?
questions.answer:
class A: def method(self): return 1. A.Method is a plain function stored in A.__dict__. In Python 3, no binding happens at class level.

code:
class A:
    def method(self):
        return 1

print(type(A.__dict__['method']).__name__)

real example:
Low-level code can reach the raw function to call it with an explicit self.

questions.question: class A: def method(self): return 1. What does A().method return (without call)?
questions.answer:
class A: def method(self): return 1. A().method (without calling it) is a bound method. Instance access wraps the function with the object.

code:
class A:
    def method(self):
        return 1

print(type(A().method).__name__)

real example:
Handing a bound method to a UI callback keeps its instance attached.

questions.question: What does A.__dict__ contain for a class with method m and class attr x?
questions.answer:
A.__dict__ is a mappingproxy containing keys for the method m and the class attribute x. Methods and class attributes both live in the class namespace.

code:
class A:
    x = 1

    def m(self):
        return 2

print('x' in A.__dict__, 'm' in A.__dict__)

real example:
Reflection tools inspect the class namespace to list its members.

questions.question: What does the @property decorator turn a method into?
class A: def __init__(self): self._v = 1; @property def v(self): return self._v. What does A().v return?
With @property only (no setter), what does a.v = 5 do?
class A: def __init__(self): self._v = 1; @property def v(self): return self._v; @v.setter def v(self, val): self._v = val * 2. What does a = A(); a.v = 5; a._v return?
What does @v.setter allow you to add?
class A: @property def v(self): return 42; @v.deleter def v(self): raise Exception('no'). What happens on del a.v?
What is the underscore convention _name for?
questions.answer:
The underscore convention _name is a soft 'protected' signal. It marks an attribute as internal, but nothing enforces it.

code:
class A:
    def __init__(self):
        self._secret = 1

real example:
Libraries mark private helpers with an underscore to warn users away.

questions.question: What does double-underscore __name do to attribute names?
questions.answer:
Double-underscore __name triggers name mangling: inside the class, __name becomes _ClassName__name. This keeps private names from colliding.

code:
class A:
    def __init__(self):
        self.__x = 1

print(A().__dict__)

real example:
Two mixins each defining __data will not overwrite each other thanks to mangling.

questions.question: class A: def __init__(self): self.__x = 1. What key is in a.__dict__ for an instance a?
questions.answer:
class A: def __init__(self): self.__x = 1. The key stored in a.__dict__ is '_A__x' because the name was mangled.

code:
class A:
    def __init__(self):
        self.__x = 1

print(A().__dict__)

real example:
Inspecting an object shows the mangled key where the hidden value lives.

questions.question: For the setup above, what does a.__x raise?
questions.answer:
a.__x raises AttributeError outside the class. Outside the body, __x is not mangled, and no such attribute exists.

code:
class A:
    def __init__(self):
        self.__x = 1

print(A().__x)

real example:
Accidental attempts to reach private state fail, nudging you toward accessors.

questions.question: Can you still access the mangled attribute from outside?
questions.answer:
Yes, you can still access the mangled attribute from outside using the full mangled name a._A__x. Mangling is a convention, not real security.

code:
class A:
    def __init__(self):
        self.__x = 1

print(A()._A__x)

real example:
Debuggers and tests peek at mangled names to inspect internal state.

questions.question: class A: __x = 5. What does A._A__x return?
questions.answer:
class A: __x = 5. A._A__x returns 5. Class-level private attributes are mangled the same way instance ones are.

code:
class A:
    __x = 5

print(A._A__x)

real example:
Class-level private counters stay hidden behind mangled names.

questions.question: class A: def __init__(self): self._v = 1. @property def v(self): return self._v. Is the property on the instance or the class?
class A: x = 1. print(hasattr(A, 'x')) outputs?
questions.answer:
class A: x = 1. print(hasattr(A, 'x')) outputs True. Classes expose their attributes to hasattr just like instances do.

code:
class A:
    x = 1

print(hasattr(A, 'x'))

real example:
Framework checks whether a model class declares a particular field.

questions.question: class A: x = 1. print(hasattr(A(), 'x')) outputs?
questions.answer:
class A: x = 1. print(hasattr(A(), 'x')) outputs True. Instances see the inherited class attribute during lookup.

code:
class A:
    x = 1

print(hasattr(A(), 'x'))

real example:
Optional-presence checks work identically for instances and classes.

questions.question: class A: x = 1. print(getattr(A, 'x')) outputs?
questions.answer:
class A: x = 1. print(getattr(A, 'x')) outputs 1. getattr also works on classes to read class attributes by name.

code:
class A:
    x = 1

print(getattr(A, 'x'))

real example:
Reading a config class attribute whose name comes from a string variable.

questions.question: What does dir(A()) list?
questions.answer:
dir(A()) lists every accessible attribute and method name, including inherited ones and dunder methods, sorted as a list. It is the object's complete public surface.

code:
class A:
    x = 1

print('x' in dir(A()))

real example:
Auto-discovering the capabilities of an imported object.

questions.question: class A: x = 1. print(sorted([a for a in dir(A()) if not a.startswith('_')])) outputs?
questions.answer:
print(sorted([a for a in dir(A()) if not a.startswith('_')])) outputs ['x']. Filtering out private and dunder names leaves only x.

code:
class A:
    x = 1

print([a for a in dir(A()) if not a.startswith('_')])

real example:
Generating an API endpoint list from public method names.

questions.question: Can two instances of the same class have different sets of attributes?
questions.answer:
Yes, two instances of the same class can have different sets of attributes. New attributes can be added to any instance independently.

code:
class A:
    pass

a = A()
a.z = 1
print(hasattr(a, 'z'), hasattr(A(), 'z'))

real example:
Some sessions need extra fields, so only those objects get them.

questions.question: class A: pass. a=A(); b=A(). a.z = 1; print('z' in b.__dict__) outputs?
questions.answer:
class A: pass. a=A(); b=A(). a.z = 1; print('z' in b.__dict__) outputs False. The z attribute exists only on a, not on b.

code:
class A:
    pass

a = A()
b = A()
a.z = 1
print('z' in b.__dict__)

real example:
Per-instance annotations stay isolated between records.

questions.question: class A: pass. a=A(); print(len(a.__dict__)) outputs?
questions.answer:
class A: pass. a=A(); print(len(a.__dict__)) outputs 0. No attributes were ever set, so the instance dictionary is empty.

code:
class A:
    pass

print(len(A().__dict__))

real example:
An unconfigured object holds no state until something assigns it.

questions.question: What does __slots__ = ['x', 'y'] do?
questions.answer:
__slots__ = ['x', 'y'] declares a fixed set of attributes and removes the per-instance __dict__, saving memory. Only listed names may exist.

code:
class A:
    __slots__ = ['x', 'y']

a = A()
a.x = 1
print(hasattr(a, '__dict__'))

real example:
Millions of lightweight records fit in memory when each skips a dict.

questions.question: class A: __slots__ = ['x']. a=A(); a.x = 1; print(a.x) outputs?
questions.answer:
class A: __slots__ = ['x']. a=A(); a.x = 1; print(a.x) outputs 1. Attributes listed in __slots__ work like normal attributes.

code:
class A:
    __slots__ = ['x']

a = A()
a.x = 1
print(a.x)

real example:
Speed-critical game entities store attributes in fixed slots.

questions.question: class A: __slots__ = ['x']. a=A(); a.z = 1 raises what?
questions.answer:
class A: __slots__ = ['x']. a.z = 1 raises AttributeError: 'A' object has no attribute 'z'. z is not allowed and there is no dict for it.

code:
class A:
    __slots__ = ['x']

a = A()
a.z = 1

real example:
Restricting fields catches typos like witdth instead of width early.

questions.question: class A: __slots__ = ['x']. print(hasattr(A(), '__dict__')) outputs?
questions.answer:
class A: __slots__ = ['x']. print(hasattr(A(), '__dict__')) outputs False. A slots class does not get a per-instance dictionary.

code:
class A:
    __slots__ = ['x']

print(hasattr(A(), '__dict__'))

real example:
Saving memory on millions of small objects by dropping dicts.

questions.question: class A: __slots__ = ['x']. print(a.x) before setting returns? (via class default)
questions.answer:
Before being set, a.x raises AttributeError unless a class-level default exists. Slots do not lazily default to None.

code:
class A:
    __slots__ = ['x']

print(A().x)

real example:
A required field will not silently read as None before being assigned.

questions.question: How do you give reasonable defaults to a slots class?
questions.answer:
Give slots their defaults inside __init__, for example self.x = default. __init__ runs for every instance and fills the slots.

code:
class A:
    __slots__ = ['x']

    def __init__(self):
        self.x = 0

print(A().x)

real example:
Every new game character starts with default health set in __init__.

questions.question: class A: __slots__ = ['x']; def __init__(self): self.x = 0. What does A().x return?
questions.answer:
class A: __slots__ = ['x']; def __init__(self): self.x = 0. A().x returns 0. __init__ stored a 0 into the slot.

code:
class A:
    __slots__ = ['x']

    def __init__(self):
        self.x = 0

print(A().x)

real example:
A counter object begins at zero for every fresh instance.

questions.question: What are the two main reasons to use __slots__?
questions.answer:
The two main reasons for __slots__ are a smaller memory footprint and faster attribute access. Skipping the dict makes objects leaner.

code:
class Point:
    __slots__ = ['x', 'y']

real example:
Graphics pipelines create millions of points; slots keep RAM low.

questions.question: What does a property prevent at Python level?
class A: x = 1. A.x = 100; print(A().x) outputs?
questions.answer:
class A: x = 1. A.x = 100; print(A().x) outputs 100. Changing the class attribute instantly affects every unshadowed instance.

code:
class A:
    x = 1

A.x = 100
print(A().x)

real example:
Raising the global tax rate updates all unpaid invoices at once.

questions.question: class A: def __init__(self): self.x = 1; self.x += 1. What does A().x return?
questions.answer:
class A: def __init__(self): self.x = 1; self.x += 1. A().x returns 2. The value is stored then incremented during initialization.

code:
class A:
    def __init__(self):
        self.x = 1
        self.x += 1

print(A().x)

real example:
A counter field increments once at record creation time.

questions.question: class A: pass. a=A(); setattr(a, 'name', 'n'); print(a.name) outputs?
questions.answer:
class A: pass. a=A(); setattr(a, 'name', 'n'); print(a.name) outputs 'n'. setattr assigns the attribute under the string name.

code:
class A:
    pass

a = A()
setattr(a, 'name', 'n')
print(a.name)

real example:
Data loaders assign fields whose names arrive as strings.

questions.question: class A: pass. a=A(); key = 'k'; setattr(a, key, 5); print(a.__dict__) outputs?
questions.answer:
class A: pass. a=A(); key = 'k'; setattr(a, key, 5); print(a.__dict__) outputs {'k': 5}. The dynamic assignment lands in the instance dict.

code:
class A:
    pass

a = A()
key = 'k'
setattr(a, key, 5)
print(a.__dict__)

real example:
Parsing CSV headers into object attributes by name.

questions.question: class A: x = 1. a=A(). What does a.__getattribute__('x') do?
questions.answer:
a.__getattribute__('x') runs the default attribute lookup and returns 1. __getattribute__ is the machinery behind all attribute access.

code:
class A:
    x = 1

print(A().__getattribute__('x'))

real example:
Framework internals call __getattribute__ to reuse the default lookup safely.

questions.question: What hook is called when an attribute is NOT found normally?
questions.answer:
The hook called when an attribute is NOT found normally is __getattr__ (if the class defines it). It runs only after the normal lookup fails.

code:
class A:
    def __getattr__(self, name):
        return 'missing'

print(A().nope)

real example:
Proxy objects forward unknown attribute names to a remote service.

questions.question: class A: def __getattr__(self, name): return f'missing:{name}'. a=A(); print(a.anything) outputs?
questions.answer:
class A: def __getattr__(self, name): return f'missing:{name}'. a=A(); print(a.anything) outputs 'missing:anything'. Any unknown name reaches __getattr__.

code:
class A:
    def __getattr__(self, name):
        return f'missing:{name}'

print(A().anything)
